stories.headline: IRAN PEACE DEAL OPTIMISM SENDS S&P 500 AND NASDAQ TO FRESH RECORDS
stories.body: The S&P 500 gained 1.46% to a record 7,365 and the Nasdaq surged 2.02% to 25,839 after Axios reported the U.S. and Iran are nearing a deal including a nuclear enrichment moratorium. All but two S&P 500 sectors finished green — Industrials led at +2.7%, Tech +2.2%; Energy cratered 4.2% as oil collapsed. Trump later cooled sentiment, calling a deal 'a big assumption.'

stories.headline: WTI CRUDE PLUNGES 7% ON IRAN CEASEFIRE REPORTS; GOLD RALLIES TO $4,697
stories.body: WTI fell to $95.18/bbl (-6.93%) and Brent dropped to $102.22/bbl (-6.96%) as markets priced out the Middle East war premium. Gold paradoxically surged to $4,697/oz (+3.11%) — cheaper oil reduces the inflation tail that has kept the Fed cautious, giving bulls a dual argument for holding both equities and bullion.

stories.headline: AGENTIC AI DEMAND SURGE POWERS AMD FORECAST REVISION; CORNING +17% ON NVIDIA OPTICAL DEAL
stories.body: AMD CEO Lisa Su told CNBC that agentic AI is 'driving tremendous demand' across the CPU cycle, justifying a major forecast revision higher. Separately, Nvidia announced a partnership with Corning for three optical manufacturing facilities in NC and TX creating 3,000+ jobs — Corning soared 17% while Nvidia added ~2%.

stories.headline: FED HELD RATES AT 3.5–3.75%; WARSH INHERITS MOST-DISSENT FOMC SINCE 1992
stories.body: At the April 29 FOMC — Powell's final meeting as chair — the Fed held the fed funds rate at 3.5–3.75% with four dissents, the most since October 1992. Three officials pushed to drop forward-guidance language; one called for an immediate cut. Kevin Warsh inherits the chair next month; his June meeting will be the first true test of his policy direction.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN CHAMPIONS ADD TOURNAMENT MOP CADEAU AND TENNESSEE TRANSFER ESTRELLA
stories.body: Tournament Most Outstanding Player Elliot Cadeau commits to return to Michigan for 2026-27, and Tennessee big man J.P. Estrella transfers to Ann Arbor. The Wolverines are stacking talent around their national title core, immediately making them a 2027 preseason contender.

stories.headline: CONFERENCE SEMIFINALS OPEN: KNICKS-76ERS AND SPURS-WOLVES GAME 2S TONIGHT; PISTONS LEAD CAVS 1-0
stories.body: Detroit won Game 1 of the East Semis 111-101 on May 5 (Cade Cunningham: 23 pts, 7 ast; Tobias Harris: 20 pts). Tonight's doubleheader features Knicks vs. 76ers (7 PM ET) and Timberwolves vs. Spurs (9:30 PM ET), with Victor Wembanyama in pursuit of an all-time playoff blocks record.

stories.headline: BENGALS LAND DEXTER LAWRENCE FOR #10 PICK; SAINTS NEAR $52M DEAL WITH ETIENNE
stories.body: Cincinnati acquired DT Dexter Lawrence from the Giants for the No. 10 overall pick, immediately signing him to a one-year, $28M extension. Post-draft free agency remains active: the Saints are nearing a 4-year, $52M deal with RB Travis Etienne, and the Lions shipped David Montgomery to Houston for OL Juice Scruggs and picks.

stories.headline: POST-SPRING TOP 25: TEXAS LEADS WITH HEALTHY ARCH MANNING; NOTRE DAME GAME DRAWS 45,308
stories.body: Post-spring way-too-early rankings have Texas atop the field — Arch Manning is healthy after offseason foot surgery, with Sarkisian's offense projected as the most explosive in the SEC. Notre Dame's Blue-Gold Game drew 45,308, the second-largest spring game crowd in program history, showcasing what scouts call the best defensive unit in college football.

deepDive.title: The Oil-Inflation Feedback Loop: Why a 7% Crude Drop Reprices Everything
content: WTI crude fell nearly 7% today on Iran peace deal optimism, and the market's reaction extended far beyond the energy sector. Understanding why requires tracing the transmission channel from oil to inflation to Fed policy to equity multiples. Oil is simultaneously a direct input cost — touching transportation, manufacturing, and chemicals — and a psychological anchor for inflation expectations. When crude drops sharply, it compresses near-term CPI and reduces what economists call 'second-round effects': wage demands that workers embed to compensate for expected energy costs. Today's sector breakdown made this explicit: Energy -4.2% while Industrials, Tech, and Materials all rallied 2%+.

The mechanism runs through what the Fed calls 'pass-through.' A sustained 10% decline in oil prices typically subtracts 0.2–0.4 percentage points from headline CPI over six months, based on BLS input-output weights. Today's single-session drop of nearly 7% represents a substantial portion of that theoretical impulse if it holds. This matters acutely right now because the FOMC is sitting at 3.5–3.75% with four dissents at its last meeting — the most since October 1992. Cheaper oil hands the doves ammunition: with energy disinflating, the case for cutting rates strengthens even if core services remain sticky. The market is essentially front-running a scenario where Kevin Warsh can cut in June without risking an inflation re-acceleration.

History offers a useful benchmark. After the 1991 Gulf War ended, WTI fell from ~$32 to ~$20 in weeks, locking in a benign CPI environment that enabled the Fed to cut aggressively through 1992–93. More recently, the 2014–2016 oil collapse — from $107 to below $27 — was so disinflationary it nearly pushed the Fed into deflation-fighting mode rather than normalization, and crushed high-yield credit where energy issuers were heavily concentrated. The paradox both then and now: collapsing oil boosts equity P/E multiples via lower discount rates and margin expansion, while simultaneously destroying earnings and credit quality in the energy sector itself. Today's bifurcation — tech and industrials bid, energy dumped — maps precisely onto that dynamic.

The key forward question is durability. A one-page memorandum is not a treaty; Trump's own caveat that a deal is 'a big assumption' signals meaningful execution risk. If the ceasefire holds, the disinflation impulse argues for the June FOMC to at least open the door to cuts, especially with Warsh arriving with political pressure to move. If talks collapse and WTI re-spikes toward $105+, today's equity gains unwind rapidly. Watch the WTI futures term structure: if front-month contracts fall while back-end contracts hold, markets are pricing a temporary war premium unwinding — a bullish signal for risk assets. If the entire curve drops, the market believes structural supply change is coming, which is a stronger and more durable tailwind for the disinflation thesis heading into summer.
